clinicalPearls: The hallmark is impaired adduction of the eye ipsilateral to the lesion with dissociated abducting nystagmus of the contralateral eye on attempted horizontal gaze
Convergence is characteristically preserved when the lesion is caudal (pontine), since the near reflex uses a separate midbrain pathway, but may be lost in rostral (midbrain) lesions
The lesion lies in the medial longitudinal fasciculus, which relays the abducens internuclear signal to the contralateral medial rectus subnucleus of the oculomotor complex
Bilateral INO in a young adult strongly suggests multiple sclerosis, whereas unilateral INO in an older patient suggests a brainstem infarct
Skew deviation with a vertical misalignment and gaze-evoked or upbeat nystagmus may accompany the horizontal deficit
Adduction lag may be subtle and best detected by observing the speed of saccades rather than the range of movement
The WEBINO variant (wall-eyed bilateral INO) shows bilateral adduction failure with exotropia in primary position
reference.pathophysiology: The medial longitudinal fasciculus carries signals from abducens internuclear neurones in the pons upward to the contralateral medial rectus subnucleus of the oculomotor nucleus, coordinating conjugate horizontal gaze. A lesion of the fasciculus interrupts this yoking so that the adducting eye fails to move while the abducting eye develops a dissociated nystagmus, thought to reflect an adaptive increase in innervation. In younger patients the commonest cause is a demyelinating plaque of multiple sclerosis, while in older patients small-vessel brainstem infarction predominates; tumour, Wernicke encephalopathy, and drug toxicity are less common causes.
additionalDifferentials: Partial oculomotor nerve palsy with medial rectus weakness
Thyroid eye disease restricting ocular motility
One-and-a-half syndrome when a horizontal gaze palsy coexists
Skew deviation from other posterior fossa pathology
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brainstem with attention to the dorsal pons and midbrain
MRI of the whole brain and spinal cord to detect demyelinating lesions
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis for oligoclonal bands when demyelination is suspected
Acetylcholine receptor antibodies and repetitive nerve stimulation to exclude myasthenia
Vascular risk assessment and stroke workup in older patients
Thiamine status where nutritional deficiency is possible
redFlags: Acute onset with other brainstem signs suggesting infarction requiring urgent stroke pathway assessment
Bilateral INO in a young patient prompting evaluation for multiple sclerosis
Associated reduced consciousness, ataxia, or ophthalmoplegia suggesting Wernicke encephalopathy
Rapidly progressive signs suggesting a mass lesion in the brainstem
reference.prognosis: Demyelinating INO frequently improves or resolves over weeks, whereas ischaemic INO has a variable outcome depending on infarct size; residual adduction lag and diplopia may persist and reflect the underlying cause more than the sign itself.
pitfalls: Attributing the adduction failure to a medial rectus palsy and missing the internuclear localisation
Overlooking myasthenia, which can perfectly mimic an INO and fluctuate
Failing to image the spinal cord and brain fully when demyelination is suspected
Missing an accompanying skew deviation or one-and-a-half syndrome that changes localisation
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Treat the underlying cause rather than the sign: corticosteroids for an acute demyelinating relapse and disease-modifying therapy for multiple sclerosis
Manage ischaemic internuclear ophthalmoplegia with stroke secondary prevention using antiplatelet therapy and vascular risk factor control
Correct thiamine deficiency promptly where Wernicke encephalopathy is possible, and treat other identified causes such as tumour or drug toxicity
Relieve symptomatic diplopia with prisms or temporary occlusion while the underlying process is treated
Investigate and monitor with neuroimaging and, where relevant, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, and exclude myasthenia gravis as a mimic
Refer to neurology and neuro-ophthalmology, coordinating long-term management of the causative disorder
